title: Orthography, Phonetics & Syllable Quantity
source: Original instructional lesson authored for this application (syllabus ref: Haywood & Nahmad Ch. 1; Ryding Ch. 2 §§2.3–2.8)
objectives: Identify short vowels (fatḥah, kasrah, ḍammah) and auxiliary signs (sukūn, shaddah, maddah).
Distinguish hamzat al-qaṭʿ (disjunctive) from hamzat al-waṣl (elidable) in connected reading.
Apply solar (shamsiyyah) and lunar (qamariyyah) assimilation rules with the definite article أَلْ.
recallPrompt: Why does Classical Arabic require vocalizing short vowel endings rather than dropping them in pause?

sections.heading: Vowels, Auxiliary Signs & Syllable Weight
sections.body: Arabic script writes its 28 consonants explicitly, while short vowels are marked above or below letters with diacritics (ḥarakāt): fatḥah (ـَ /a/), kasrah (ـِ /i/), and ḍammah (ـُ /u/). Sukūn (ـْ) marks a vowelless consonant, shaddah (ـّ) doubles a consonant, and maddah (آ) represents a long /ā/ following hamzah.

sections.label: Solar vs. Lunar Assimilation
sections.summary: Before the 14 solar letters (ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن), the lām of أَلْ assimilates completely into the following consonant, which takes shaddah. Before the 14 lunar letters, the lām is pronounced clearly with sukūn.

sections.heading: Solar, Lunar & Hamzah Signs
rows: Lām is pronounced clearly with sukūn
Lām is silent; ش doubles with shaddah
Elides after a preceding vowel in connected speech

sections.irab: الشَّمْسُ: لَامٌ شَمْسِيَّةٌ مُدْغَمَةٌ | وَالقَمَرُ: هَمْزَةُ وَصْلٍ تَسْقُطُ فِي الدَّرْجِ
sections.notes: In connected reading, the hamzat al-waṣl on القَمَرُ drops after وَ, linking directly: wa-l-qamaru.

sections.heading: Qur'anic Reading Habit
sections.body: Always read shaddah as two full consonant beats (e.g., أَلشَّمْسُ = ash-shamsu, not a-shamsu). Dropping a shaddah changes word meaning and root structure.
